title: TCP: connections, ports, states
summary: How a TCP connection opens, what a socket is, and how to read the states that ss shows.

text: Before any data, TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake.
- Then TCP numbers every byte, resends what's lost, and delivers in order.
- Most web traffic, SSH and databases use TCP. DNS queries and video calls mostly use UDP: no connection, no resending.
A connection is four numbers: both addresses and both ports.
- The server's port names the service (443 is HTTPS).
- The client's port is picked by the kernel, a free ephemeral one: that's how one machine holds many connections to the same server.
ss lists the sockets: -t TCP, -a all states, -n numbers (its Recv-Q and Send-Q columns are cut here).
- LISTEN: a server waiting. ESTAB: an open connection. TIME-WAIT: just closed, kept a moment.
- ss -tln shows only the listening ones; add -p to see the program.
The two classic failures tell different stories.
- Refused comes back at once: the machine is there, the port is closed. Check the server started, and on which address.
- Timed out takes long, up to about two minutes: nothing answers. Look at firewalls and routes.
